title: Module System
concept: Module declaration organizes code into named namespaces
why: As programs grow beyond a single file, organizing code into logical groups becomes essential. Modules provide namespace isolation, preventing name collisions and making code discoverable. Without modules, all symbols would live in a flat global namespace — unmaintainable at scale.
theory: A module in XIOM is declared with the `mod` keyword followed by the module name and a block of code. Modules create a hierarchy: code inside a module uses its local namespace, and symbols are accessed from outside using the `::` path separator. Module files map to the filesystem — a module `mod math` expects either `math.xi` alongside the parent or `math/mod.xi` for nested modules. XIOM's module system is inspired by Rust but simpler: no `mod.rs` convention; every module is either inline or a single file.
tips: Use `mod` blocks at the top of your file before function definitions
Think of `::` like a slash in a file path — it drills into the module tree
common_mistakes: Forgetting `pub` on items meant to be used outside the module
Using `.` instead of `::` to access module members
Declaring modules after they are used in the file
